headline: Barefoot Walk Turns Into Pygmy Rattlesnake Nightmare for 7-Year-Old in Keystone Heights
summary: A 7-year-old girl is recovering after a pygmy rattlesnake bit her bare foot in a sandy Keystone Heights yard. Her message: wear shoes.
body:
SnakeNews, SnakeNews. Stop what you are doing and look down at your feet. In Keystone Heights, Florida, a barefoot walk across a sandy yard turned into a terrifying medical emergency for a seven-year-old girl. She is recovering tonight after a pygmy rattlesnake bite, and her message to every kid and every parent is as simple as it is urgent: wear shoes.

The story begins about three weeks ago, when the girl was walking to her grandmother's house, just a short distance away. Her sister told her to wait, and five seconds later, the snake struck. The girl told WCJB, "My sister told me, wait. And five seconds later, I turned around. The snake just came and bit me."

She never saw it coming. She did not even realize what had happened at first. Then she looked down. In her words, "I noticed it after. I looked at the ground when it bit me. It was black with white polka dots." That description has snake experts nodding grimly: pygmy rattlesnakes are masters of disappearing into sand, gravel, and pine straw. The girl was bitten in a sandy area, exactly the kind of place this small venomous snake calls home.

Her family had never dealt with a snakebite before. The girl said, "I was like, 'What happened to my foot? I don't know what happened,' and I was not guessing it was a snake because none of our family has been bit by a snake." But when she screamed, her mother came outside. At first, the mother did not know it was a snakebite either. They brought her inside, looked at her foot, and the question came: "Is that a snake bite?" The girl answered, "Yeah."

From there, the family rushed her to get medical care. She was crying and scared, and she spent a long and difficult stretch in the hospital. At the first hospital, she received an IV and some antivenom over about eight hours, but it was not enough. Doctors transferred her to a second hospital for a second, stronger dose. In total, she spent two nights and three days in the hospital before finally going home.

The pain did not disappear when the antivenom went in. The girl described the feeling this way: "My whole body was like shaking, kind of like dancing, but in a bad way. And it was just hurting." For a time, she could move her leg but not her entire foot. She said she could move past her knee but could not move her whole foot. It was a frightening recovery for a child who also missed her brothers and sisters while she was away.

Now, three weeks after the bite, the girl is feeling much better, with only a small amount of bruising left. She has a simple piece of advice for other kids, and it is worth repeating until it sticks: "Wear shoes."

And now, the SnakeNews Safety Desk. Let us be clear about what we are dealing with here. The pygmy rattlesnake, sometimes called the ground rattler, is a small but venomous pit viper found across the southeastern United States, including Florida. It rarely grows much longer than two feet, and its rattle is so tiny and soft that you might not hear it at all. This snake loves sandy, scrubby, pine flatwoods and areas near water. It sits still, blends in, and strikes when a bare foot or hand gets too close. In Florida, it is one of the snakes you are most likely to meet if you spend time outdoors in the wrong shoes.

SnakeNews Senior Reptile Correspondent Rex Scales put it this way: "A pygmy rattlesnake doesn't want to hurt you. It wants you to leave it alone. But if you step on it with no shoes, that snake is going to defend itself. The best defense for you is boots or closed shoes and watching where you put your feet."

If you or someone you are with is bitten by a pygmy rattlesnake, or any venomous snake, the SnakeNews Safety Desk wants you to remember these steps. Call 911 immediately. Stay as calm as you can. Keep the bitten arm or leg still, and keep it at the level of your heart if possible. Remove any rings or tight clothing near the bite before swelling starts. Do not use a tourniquet. Do not cut the wound. Do not try to suck out the venom. Do not ice the area. And do not chase or capture the snake. The only thing that matters is getting to a hospital for antivenom, exactly what this family did.

Now, the Santa Monica check-in. Philip, if you are reading this one aloud, tell Dad and Uncle the following: the snake in this story is a pygmy rattlesnake, a southeastern snake that does not live in Santa Monica. There are no reports of any snake coming for you today. Philip checked in with us a short time ago, and he is fine. His shoes are on. His feet are safe. His dad and uncle can breathe.

From the SnakeNews newsroom, this is your reminder to look before you step and wear real shoes in snake country. For now, we are signing off, but we will be back the moment another snake makes news. Stay safe out there.
